1.pericope_label: Who hath believed our report: he is despised and rejected of men, a man of sorrows

schools.summary: Works the crux of the pronoun and the tenses, fixing the watching eye on Jehovah, contrasting the frail sapling with the vigorous shoot from David's root, and correcting the second verb to forsaken while insisting that the words for sorrow imply bodily disease.
Makes the report the gospel itself, prefers the figure of a sucker from which nothing is hoped, and reads the growing up as a mean entrance into the world rather than a rise from low estate to high.

Identifies the arm with the Messiah in whom the power of God was seated, refers the growth to the unbelieving Jews who witnessed his mean original, and presses the received text at one point to the length of rewriting it.

Laments that of the many who hear so few believe, and supplies the social history of the humiliation, a royal family sunk, a carpenter for a supposed father, and a face worn beyond its years with grief.

debates.question: Before whom did the servant grow up?

positions.view: before Jehovah, who is named immediately before, so that the growth went on under his eye though men did not observe it
before the unbelieving Jews of the preceding verse, who were witnesses of his mean original and despised him for it

debates.question: What is the arm of the Lord that was not revealed?

positions.view: the divine power accompanying the word, made bare in the miracles that confirmed the doctrine and in its force upon the conscience, unperceived by those who had forfeited grace
the Messiah himself, so called because the almighty power of God was seated in him, revealed inwardly and with power
not the arm at all, since no arm can be said to grow up; the word differs by a letter from the one meaning seed, and should be read of Christ alone

outliers.reading: Alone takes up the question whether the servant's body could be subject to disease, calls the a priori denial idle, and answers that such subjection was an essential condition of his fellowship with our humanity.
Alone reports the tradition that he was never seen to laugh, and that grief so wore him that at little over thirty he was taken for nearly fifty.

themes: Who hath believed our report? and to whom is the arm of the Lord revealed?
For he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground: he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him.
He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not.

4.pericope_label: Surely he hath borne our griefs: the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all

schools.summary: Settles the particle, the tense and the case: the opening word is affirmative because the verse's own halves carry the contrast, the passives show that the wounding describes a death rather than a life, and the nouns mean sickness and pain.
Reads the confession as that of the elect, Jew and Gentile, sheep unable to return until they are brought back, and traces the griefs to the sinless infirmities Christ took with the nature.

States the false verdict of the onlookers plainly and the substitution vividly, the burden made to meet on him as rivers meet in the sea, or as rays deflected from every quarter converge in one focus.
Unfolds why men inferred divine anger from the suffering, and presses the healing beyond pardon, sin being a disease of the soul for which the stripes purchased the grace that mortifies it.

debates.question: Who are the all we that went astray like sheep?

positions.view: the elect of God, Jew and Gentile alike, compared to sheep for their stupidity and their inability to return of themselves
all mankind, turned in general to the way of sin and in particular to the several paths different men choose
restored Israel looking back on the exile, the final state of punishment before deliverance, a scattered flock that had lost the way
both at once, the confession of repentant Israel and of repentant humanity

debates.question: What are the griefs and sorrows he bore?

positions.view: sickness and pain, so that the evangelist's use of the verse for bodily healings is entirely legitimate
readable also as our sins, following the Greek and the apostle who quotes it, since our griefs are owing to our sins and deserved by them

outliers.reading: Alone gives the substitution an optical figure, the fiery rays that should have fallen on all mankind deflected from east, west, north and south and converged upon one focal point.
Alone sets beside the false verdict the friends of a much earlier sufferer, who likewise esteemed him smitten of God because there was something uncommon in his affliction.

themes: Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted.
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.

7.pericope_label: He opened not his mouth: cut off out of the land of the living, and with the rich in his death

schools.summary: Takes the verbs at their strongest, hard pressed and hunted, hurried out of the midst of suffering rather than away from it, and reads the burial clause by the law of parallelism against the traditional application.
Turns the opening into a legal transaction, satisfaction exacted and answered by the surety, and keeps the burial as commonly told, noting that the clauses fit exactly if transposed.

Supports its readings from custom and antiquity, the crier who invited witnesses to a condemned man's innocence and the heaped mound that made a tomb a high place, and keeps the silence and the yielding voluntary.

debates.question: What does it mean that he made his grave with the wicked and with the rich in his death?

positions.view: the familiar fulfilment, crucified between thieves and buried in a rich man's tomb; the clauses fit exactly if transposed, or else both rich and wicked were concerned about the grave
not an honourable burial at all: parallelism requires the rich to answer the wicked and so to mean the wrongfully rich, so that men assigned him an oppressor's grave, whom nobody lamented
the disputed word is a noun meaning heights, since old tombs were heaped mounds set on eminences, so that his high place is simply his tomb
with the wicked denotes sameness of condition rather than of place, and he made his grave because the yielding was his own act
his contemporaries: as to that generation, who will consider rightly, since what follows names the very fact they failed to consider
his posterity, the numberless multitude who would believe, promised him as the reward of his willingness to be cut off
his manner of life, which the rule required a crier to invite witnesses to defend, a benefit nobody offered at this trial

outliers.reading: Alone doubts that a clandestine funeral without public lamentation could be an adequate recognition of the victim's holiness, and reads the concessive clause as although rather than because.
Alone renders the opening clause as an exaction answered, the surety called on for the debt and paying it to the last farthing before the bond was cancelled.

themes: He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth.
He was taken from prison and from judgment: and who shall declare his generation? for he was cut off out of the land of the living: for the transgression of my people was he stricken.
And he made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death; because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth.

10.pericope_label: It pleased the LORD to bruise him: he shall see of the travail of his soul and be satisfied

schools.summary: Refers the bruising to the Father's good pleasure rather than to chance or the persecutors, insists on the trespass offering as a satisfaction proportioned to the sin, and welcomes a phrase for knowledge that carries both its senses at once.
Speaks most strongly of what the bruising involved, the wrath of God coming upon him for the sins laid on him, and keeps both the satisfaction and the promised portion personal to the servant.
Divides the causes of the suffering, weighs the textual witnesses, and reads the promised length of days of the spiritual progeny, adding a historical claim about the growth of the faith since.
Draws a careful line at the wrath of God, which it says scripture nowhere ascribes to these sufferings, and keeps the household image, a father who will not commit so numerous a family to another.

debates.question: How far may it be pressed that it pleased the Lord to bruise him?

positions.view: to its full extent: when the sins of his people were laid on him the wrath of God came upon him for them, and the sufferings were predetermined and in a manner delighted in
not so far: scripture nowhere says Christ underwent the wrath of God, only that the Lord bruised him, awakened his own sword and put the bitter cup into his hand
God was the principal cause of the sufferings though men's sins were the deserving cause
the sufferings are referred not to chance or fate or the wickedness of persecutors but to the absolute good pleasure of the Father, fullest in the hour of apparent failure
the servant himself, who unlike men content to depart when they see their children's children will not commit so numerous a household to another
the servant, in that he shall live and reign with God for ever
the spiritual progeny rather than the person, the promise being that Christianity shall endure to the end of time

outliers.reading: Alone adds a historical claim of his own to the exposition, that every succeeding century has so far witnessed more Christianity in the world than the one before it.
Alone insists on the technical distinction between the trespass offering and the sin offering, so that the death carries the idea not of atonement only but of a satisfaction proportioned to the sin.

themes: Yet it pleased the Lord to bruise him; he hath put him to grief: when thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed, he shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of the Lord shall prosper in his hand.
He shall see of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied: by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many; for he shall bear their iniquities.

Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong; because he hath poured out his soul unto death: and he was numbered with the transgressors; and he bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
